Chapter One: Understanding the State as a Tool of Class Power
Let’s start by asking a pretty big question—what is the state, really? And why does it even exist?
Now, it’s easy to picture the state as some sort of neutral umpire, standing above all the messy parts of society and making sure everything’s fair. But, if we look a little closer, we see that’s just not the case. The state is actually a complex system of power, carefully structured to keep one social class on top of the rest.
This idea is at the heart of the Marxist view of politics and history.
Picture society as an open field, crowded with different groups—workers, business owners, landowners—all competing for resources, influence, and control. In this constant contest, the state takes shape as a collection of institutions: governments, courts, police, armies, and all those layers of bureaucracy.
But here’s the thing—these aren’t just there to keep the peace. They’re built to enforce the interests of whichever class happens to hold economic power at the moment. So, when capitalists own the factories, the banks, and the land, the state’s rules and force get used to protect their property and their privileges.
That flips the common idea on its head, doesn’t it? The state isn’t an even-handed guardian for everyone. Instead, it’s more like a fortress—built and maintained to defend the ruling class from anyone who might challenge their position. Think about it: when police aren’t just stopping crime, but breaking up strikes or shutting down protests that threaten business as usual. Or when courts don’t just settle disputes, but interpret laws in ways that quietly tip the scales toward those with money and connections.
This isn’t just a theory. If we look back through history, every major state has sprung up alongside deep divisions in society. In ancient times, the state protected slave owners. Feudal societies? The state shielded the nobility. And in today’s capitalist world, it’s all about defending the interests of business owners.
At its core, the state’s main job is to manage and contain the conflicts that naturally come from these divisions—using laws, and when that isn’t enough, using force.
So, let’s break down a few key points that really clarify this way of thinking:
First, the state is born out of deep, irreconcilable antagonisms between social classes. It comes into existence when society splits into groups with interests that just can’t be squared.
Second, its main purpose isn’t to mediate fairly between everyone. It’s there to maintain the dominance of the class in power.
And finally, the state uses both legal authority—and, when needed, the threat or reality of violence—to shut down challenges from below.
Seeing the state this way really changes things, doesn’t it? Suddenly, the idea that we can simply reform the state from within—by passing better laws or electing new leaders—starts to look pretty shaky. The machinery of the state is built to serve the powerful, and it’s designed to resist any real change that could knock them off the top.
So, understanding the state as an instrument of class rule isn’t just an academic point—it’s the foundation for thinking about what real transformation would take. Not just shuffling the people in charge, but actually changing the whole structure of society itself.
